title: Fra Angelico's cells
hookLine: each friar's cell at San Marco has its own fresco to pray with

cards: A stone staircase in an old friary in Florence. You climb it, turn at the top, and on the wall in front of you is an angel, wings striped like a bird's, bowing to a young woman on a bench.
Mary leans forward, arms crossed over her chest, listening. The colors are soft, the room plain, almost empty.
Then you walk down the corridor, and every small doorway opens on a bare room with a single window and one more painting on the wall. A different one in each.
This is San Marco, and the painter was a friar who lived there.

teach.b: You met the painter back on day eight hundred thirty-four; today, why his rooms look the way they do. He was a Dominican, Fra Giovanni, remembered as Fra Angelico, the angelic brother.
With his workshop he painted frescoes on the walls of the friars' cells, the small rooms where each brother slept, studied and prayed. These were not made for visitors.

teach.h: MADE FOR ONE FRIAR AT A TIME.
teach.b: They were made for one man at a time, to pray with, alone. So they are quiet on purpose: few details, plain backgrounds, nothing to distract. And in several of them there's a surprise.
Off to the side of the Gospel scene stands a Dominican friar, sometimes Saint Dominic himself, simply watching.

teach.h: A FRIAR STANDS INSIDE THE SCENE.
teach.b: The friar in his cell looks at the wall and sees a friar inside the story: this is where you belong, at the edge of the scene, paying attention. At the top of the stairs, the Annunciation sets the tone for the house.
Luke's Gospel gives Mary's answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." Listening, then yes.

teach.h: THIS WEEK: DOMINICANS IN MANY CLOTHES.
teach.b: That's the Dominican rhythm this week has followed in different clothes: Rose and Martin in Lima, an honest look at the Inquisition, Lacordaire back in France, laypeople with a study group, a climber in Turin, a theologian who waited.

teach.h: BE IT DONE TO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.
teach.b: And here, a painter who gave each brother a window into the Gospel, right next to his real window.

how: Some Catholics keep an icon, a crucifix or a holy picture in the place they pray at home, and San Marco in Florence, now a museum, still shows Fra Angelico's frescoes in the friars' cells.

games.q: you're painting a fresco for a brother's cell, the room he'll pray in every day. what do you paint?
o: a crowded, dazzling scene full of detail.
a quiet Gospel scene with a friar praying at its edge.
a portrait of the prior who paid for it.
games.why: the cell frescoes are spare on purpose, and several put a Dominican inside the scene, at the edge, paying attention.

practice: Look around your space and choose one spot at eye level: a shelf, a corner of a desk, the wall beside your bed.

Picture what could go there, a small icon, a print, a photo, and for now just look at the spot and breathe, the way a friar might sit with his wall. If you pray, let Mary's answer, be it done to me, rest there.

wordCard.voice: Fra Angelico's cells. The rooms at San Marco in Florence, each with its own quiet fresco, painted by a Dominican friar for his brothers to pray with. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a painting in each cell. Pray, study, share, and sometimes the sharing is a wall. See you tomorrow.
